topics: Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private tradeoffs
transcript:
Meeting header:
2026-08-12 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~42 minutes
Attendees: Alex Chen (Redwood AE), Priya Nambiar (Redwood SE), Daniel Park (Silverleaf CTO), Maya Lopez (Silverleaf Head of Security), Ethan Brooks (Platform Eng), Lina Ortega (Product)

Summary: quick intro, then dug into security posture & compliance requirements for PHI workloads. Conversation included network diagrams, certs, and tradeoffs between hosted/dedicated/private. Several documents referenced: redwood security pack (link), SOC2 pdf, network diagram.

00:00 Alex Chen: hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood Inference, I'm the AE working with Silverleaf, with me is Priya our solutions engineer.
00:07 Daniel Park: hey thanks Alex, yeah appreciate it, we've been looking at you all for ops infra, we want to get into security before we move to a pilot.
00:15 Priya Nambiar: quick agenda, we wanted to confirm scope is security posture and compliance for your PHI use case; talk through hosted vs dedicated vs private options; and map next steps for artifacts and benchmarks.
00:30 Maya Lopez: correct, our legal and security teams need to know SOC2/ISO status, encryption at rest, KMS integration, SSO and RBAC controls, and how audit logs are retained. Also network egress and VPC peering options.
00:45 Alex Chen: totally, we can cover all of that. Just to set context: Redwood offers hosted API, Redwood Dedicated (reserved GPU pools), and Redwood Private (VPC or on-prem private control plane). We'll go through the security controls available in each.
01:05 Ethan Brooks: quick question, how often do you rotate keys and do you support customer-managed KMS? If we're sending PHI we need control.
01:15 Priya Nambiar: yes, for Private we support customer-managed KMS with HSM-backed providers; for Dedicated we have the option to integrate with your KMS if on supported clouds; hosted offers encryption at rest with provider-managed KMS by default, but we can enable customer-managed keys for enterprise accounts under contract. Rotation cadence is configurable; we provide logs for key access.
01:40 Maya Lopez: do you have SOC 2 and ISO certs right now?
01:45 Alex Chen: we have SOC 2 Type II and ISO 27001 certificates. I'll share redacted copies after the call. The security pack link is in the notes - but we'll email the certs and the network diagram.
01:58 Daniel Park: great. For SSO we use Okta and we provision via SCIM, we need SAML 2.0 for SSO and SCIM for provisioning.
02:07 Priya Nambiar: Okta is widely used by our customers. We support SAML 2.0 for SSO and SCIM for user provisioning; RBAC can be synced from your IdP groups, and we support fine-grained roles. For Private deployments you control the IdP connection; for hosted accounts we support SAML and SCIM integrations into our control plane with enterprise SSO config.
02:30 Lina Ortega: about audit logs — how granular are they? We need to trace who called what model, token-level metrics, and any data accessed for compliance audits.
02:40 Alex Chen: logs include per-request metadata: timestamp, calling user/role, route/model version, request id, and high-level token usage. For higher fidelity we can capture request/response hashes and store them in your log bucket in Private or Dedicated. Hosted can stream logs to your SIEM via secure forwarders. Retention is configurable based on plan.
02:58 Maya Lopez: retention windows — we have to keep certain logs for 7 years for audits, is that possible?
03:05 Priya Nambiar: retention for 7 years is doable in Private — you manage lifecycle; for Dedicated we can support long retention via customer buckets; for hosted there are limits on default retention but enterprise add-ons can extend it, though long-term archival may be done to customer-managed storage. We'll capture the options in writing.
03:30 Daniel Park: any concerns with PHI in hosted? We prefer private by default but open to hosted if it meets controls.
03:38 Alex Chen: understood. Hosted is simplest but has more shared control; Dedicated gives you isolated GPU pools with network restrictions and predictable throughput; Private gives you full control (VPC, customer KMS, airgap options). For PHI, a common pattern is start with a hosted pilot with data redaction/synthetic data, then move to Dedicated or Private for production.
04:05 Ethan Brooks: can you describe network topology for Private? e.g., is there a control plane we call out to, or is everything inside our VPC?
04:13 Priya Nambiar: Private has a customer-managed control plane option; you can run control plane components in your VPC or have a hybrid where control plane is in Redwood but data plane stays in your VPC. We'll provide the architecture diagram. There are also on-prem appliances for fully air-gapped installs.
04:40 Maya Lopez: do you support FIPS 140-2 HSMs? We have regulatory constraints.
04:45 Priya Nambiar: yes, for Private we can integrate with FIPS-compliant HSMs through supported KMS providers. For Dedicated we can discuss options depending on cloud region and provider. Hosted defaults to provider-managed keys which may or may not be FIPS; for hard requirements Private is the path.
05:05 Daniel Park: what about role-based access control, separation of duties, and admin audit? We need admin actions to be auditable and limited.
05:15 Alex Chen: RBAC supports layered roles: org admin, app admin, viewer, and custom roles. All admin actions are logged. For Private you can hook into your SIEM and have fine-grained routing of audit events; we also support SSO enforced 2FA via your IdP.
05:38 Lina Ortega: is there support for model governance — e.g., version pinning, can we prevent certain models from being used in production?
05:45 Priya Nambiar: yes, model catalog and rollout controls let you pin versions per route. You can restrict which models a tenant or route can call, and we have canary rollouts and AB testing with automatic rollback. That's part of the Redwood Console.
06:05 Maya Lopez: curious about data retention: inputs & outputs — can we opt to not persist request/response content? We want only minimal logs for auditing.
06:15 Alex Chen: yes — you can opt out of storing request/response content and only retain metadata. For Private/Dedicated you control persistence; for hosted we provide settings to redact or not store payloads, and you can configure export to your storage for archival.
06:35 Daniel Park: are there legal agreements for data processing / BAA for PHI?
06:40 Alex Chen: we do sign BAAs for customers handling PHI; that flows through our enterprise legal and account team. I'll flag our legal team to open the BAA once you indicate intent.
06:55 Maya Lopez: what about penetration testing and external audits?
07:00 Priya Nambiar: we run annual external security assessments and pen tests; summaries are included in the security pack. For Private we can sign an NDA and coordinate deeper testing in your environment if required.
07:18 Ethan Brooks: SDKs and CLI — where do credentials live on our side? We want ephemeral tokens and short TTLs.
07:25 Alex Chen: tokens support short TTLs; we also support session-based short-lived creds via STS and can integrate with your identity broker for ephemeral access. CLI creds are recommended to be stored in your secret manager.
07:45 Lina Ortega: curious about isolation for Dedicated — is it single-tenant at infra level or logical multi-tenant?
07:50 Priya Nambiar: Dedicated gives reserved GPU capacity for your org and network isolation; however control plane may be shared unless you purchase Private. For strict tenant isolation you go with Private. We can document the isolation model.
08:12 Daniel Park: are audit logs tamper-evident? We need chain of custody for forensic purposes.
08:18 Priya Nambiar: logs can be shipped to an append-only storage in your cloud account; we support signed log envelopes and integration with immutable storage/lifecycle rules for forensic chain of custody.
08:38 Maya Lopez: what encryption algorithms are used in transit? TLS 1.2/1.3?
08:42 Alex Chen: TLS 1.2 and 1.3 supported, we enforce TLS for all network traffic. Internal service-to-service also uses mTLS in Private deployments.
09:00 Daniel Park: any limitations on data residency — can we ensure data doesn't leave eu-west-1?
09:06 Priya Nambiar: yes, regional routing policies allow requests to be pinned to a region. For hosted we have region-specific endpoints; for Dedicated/Private you can run in your cloud region and ensure data residency. We'll provide the region matrix.
09:28 Lina Ortega: regarding logs retention again, for hosted what's typical SLA on retrieval?
09:33 Alex Chen: hosted logs are available via console and exported streams; retrieval SLA varies by plan; we'll include specifics with pricing and SLA docs.
09:50 Maya Lopez: okay on compliance docs — can you send your SOC 2 report and ISO cert?
09:55 Alex Chen: yes, will share redacted copies and the security pack link.
10:04 Ethan Brooks: on the benchmarking you mentioned — can Redwood run a small test with our sample prompt set to show latency numbers in hosted mode? We want to see real token counts and costs.
10:12 Priya Nambiar: absolutely. If you send a representative set of payloads (anonymized), we can run them in hosted and return latency p50/p95, and estimated token costs. We'll also simulate Dedicated throughput numbers.
10:28 Daniel Park: perfect. For timeline, we want to have a pilot decision in two weeks and a production target in Q4.
10:34 Alex Chen: that sounds reasonable. We'll prioritize the SOC2/ISO docs and the benchmark. We'll also propose a pilot plan for Private evaluation if you need it.
10:45 Maya Lopez: any questions from your side on our policies? We use Okta, AWS KMS, and have a default 7-year log retention for some records; we also require FIPS HSM for long term key custody.
10:58 Priya Nambiar: noted. FIPS HSM for Private is possible. For KMS we can support AWS KMS customer-managed keys. Retention windows we'll map to the deployment options.
11:18 Lina Ortega: one last question, do you offer indemnities or security SLAs?
11:22 Alex Chen: we have enterprise SLAs and indemnity language in our contracts; legal can share standard terms — we can surface those with the BAA.
11:35 Daniel Park: ok thanks everyone, that was helpful.
11:40 Alex Chen: recap: Alex to share security artifacts and network diagram; Priya to run benchmark; Maya to send retention and required artifact list; we'll schedule pilot follow-up.
11:55 Meeting ends.

Notes / Links referenced: https://redwood.example.com/security-pack (security pack), SOC2 redacted (will be emailed), network-diagram.pdf (to be shared), benchmark spreadsheet (will be created by Priya).
